title: Standards and common protocols
starter: List every acronym you already associate with the internet. Which ones do you think are rules for sending data, and which are something else?
starterAnswer: Accept any sensible attempt: this is a hook, not an assessment.
Look for the vocabulary from the lesson objectives appearing in students' own words.
Students who are stuck should still write something: the experience will correct it.
starterNote: Take two or three answers, then leave it open. Come back to it in the plenary, when they can answer it properly.

stations.name: Standards
facts: Agreed rules and specifications so hardware and software from different makers work together.
Examples: USB, Wi-Fi (IEEE 802.11), Ethernet and HTML.
Without standards, devices couldn't talk to each other.
stations.challenge: What would happen if every phone maker used a different charging connector?
challengeAnswer: Model answer: Agreed rules and specifications so hardware and software from different makers work together.
Also credit: Examples: USB, Wi-Fi (IEEE 802.11), Ethernet and HTML.

questions.q: Why are standards needed in computing?
questions.a: So hardware and software from different manufacturers can work together

questions.q: Which of these is a standard?

stations.name: Protocols
facts: A protocol is a set of rules that governs how devices communicate on a network.
It covers the format of data, addressing and how errors are handled.
stations.challenge: What is the difference between a standard and a protocol?
challengeAnswer: Model answer: A protocol is a set of rules that governs how devices communicate on a network.
Also credit: It covers the format of data, addressing and how errors are handled.

questions.a: A set of rules for how devices communicate on a network

questions.q: Why must both devices use the same protocol?
questions.a: So each can understand the data the other sends

stations.name: Web protocols
facts: HTTP (Hypertext Transfer Protocol): a client-server way of requesting and delivering HTML files.
HTTPS (Hypertext Transfer Protocol Secure): adds encryption and authentication.
Look for the padlock in your browser.
stations.challenge: Why should a shopping website use HTTPS rather than HTTP?
challengeAnswer: Model answer: HTTP (Hypertext Transfer Protocol): a client-server way of requesting and delivering HTML files.
Also credit: HTTPS (Hypertext Transfer Protocol Secure): adds encryption and authentication.

questions.a: Requesting and delivering web pages between browsers and web servers

questions.q: What does HTTPS add to HTTP?
questions.a: Encryption and authentication of the data between client and server

stations.name: Email protocols
facts: SMTP (Simple Mail Transfer Protocol) sends email to a mail server.
POP (Post Office Protocol) retrieves email from a mail server.
IMAP (Internet Message Access Protocol) retrieves email and manages it on the server, so it syncs across devices.
stations.challenge: Why is IMAP better than POP if you read email on a phone and a laptop?
challengeAnswer: Model answer: SMTP (Simple Mail Transfer Protocol) sends email to a mail server.
Also credit: POP (Post Office Protocol) retrieves email from a mail server.

questions.q: Match each email protocol to its job.
questions.a: SMTP → Sends email to a mail server; POP → Retrieves email from a mail server; IMAP → Retrieves email and manages mailboxes on the server

questions.q: Which protocol keeps your emails in sync across your phone and laptop?

stations.name: FTP
facts: File Transfer Protocol: sends files between computers.
Often used to upload web pages and their files to a web server for hosting.
stations.challenge: A web designer has finished a site. Which protocol might they use to put it on the web server?
challengeAnswer: Model answer: File Transfer Protocol: sends files between computers.
Also credit: Often used to upload web pages and their files to a web server for hosting.

questions.q: Which protocol would upload a website's files to a web server?

stations.name: TCP/IP
facts: TCP (Transmission Control Protocol): splits data into packets and makes sure they all arrive, error-free and in order.
IP (Internet Protocol): routes packets across a wide area network using IP addresses.
stations.challenge: What would happen to a web page if some packets went missing and nothing checked?
challengeAnswer: Model answer: TCP (Transmission Control Protocol): splits data into packets and makes sure they all arrive, error-free and in order.
Also credit: IP (Internet Protocol): routes packets across a wide area network using IP addresses.

questions.a: Makes sure all the packets arrive without errors and in the right order
Routes packets across networks to the right address

final.name: Final challenge: protocol match

questions.q: Match each protocol to its description.
questions.a: HTTP → Requests and delivers web pages (HTML files); HTTPS → Web pages with encryption and authentication; FTP → Sends files between computers; SMTP → Sends email to a mail server; POP → Retrieves email from a mail server; IMAP → Retrieves email and manages mailboxes on the server; TCP → Error-free transmission of packets; IP → Routes packets across a WAN

final.note: Students should have predicted these on the worksheet before tapping the star. Mark the prediction, not just the final answer.

exam.q: Explain why agreed standards matter when devices from different makers connect.
points: Agreed rules and specifications so hardware and software from different makers work together.
Without standards, devices couldn't talk to each other.
A protocol is a set of rules that governs how devices communicate on a network.
Accept any other correct point relevant to the question.
exam.note: One mark per point, to a maximum of 3.

exam.q: Name the protocol used to send email to a mail server.
points: SMTP (Simple Mail Transfer Protocol) sends email to a mail server.
POP (Post Office Protocol) retrieves email from a mail server.
Accept any other correct point relevant to the question.
exam.note: One mark for a correct answer.

exam.q: Describe what HTTPS adds to HTTP and why it matters.
points: HTTPS (Hypertext Transfer Protocol Secure): adds encryption and authentication.
Accept any other correct point relevant to the question.
exam.note: One mark per point, to a maximum of 3.

exam.q: Explain how TCP and IP work together when a web page is requested.
points: Agreed rules and specifications so hardware and software from different makers work together.
Accept any other correct point relevant to the question.
exam.note: One mark per point, to a maximum of 4.

common: Naming a term without saying what it does: most questions need the term and its purpose.
Answering 'it's faster' or 'it's better' with no reason: link it to the characteristic the question is about.
Repeating the question in the answer and stopping there.
